en: The Fourteenth Chapter of the *Lushan Lianzong Baojian*: Discourse on the True Cause of Buddha-Recitation.
Discourse on the True Cause of Buddha-Recitation.
I have heard that among the Tathāgatas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, Amitābha is foremost;
among the Buddha-fields as vast as the motes of dust throughout the ten directions, Sukhāvatī is the ultimate refuge.
The ultimate truth is fundamentally nothing but the mind alone; its initial gateway must necessarily rely upon the ground of cultivation.
Thus we know that a tree large enough to encircle an embrace originates from a mere hair-tip, and a journey of a thousand li begins with the first step.
Desiring to transcend birth and death, one takes the Pure Land as the means for one’s ultimate destination;
intending to realize nirvana, mindfulness of the Buddha is the essential method for rectifying the mind.
One must have deep faith that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is the wondrous gateway to true liberation.
Contemplate Amitābha as truly the compassionate father of all sentient beings.
First clarify the point of arrival, and thus cultivate the cause by looking toward the fruit;
gradually tread the profound path, proceeding from cause to fruit.
Thus we know that there was a profound purpose in gathering a multitude of sages to form a society;
it was to specialize in the practice of *nianfo* (mindfulness of the Buddha) to exhort others and promote the Dharma.
Consequently, the ocean of the fruition encompasses the causal stage, and the source of the cause is thoroughly realized in the fruition.
When the form is straight, the shadow is invariably upright;
when the sound is harmonious, the resonance naturally follows.
This principle demonstrates the essential method for attaining perfect penetration through the manifestation of its power.
The World-Honored One has taught the causes for cultivating pure karma:
ascending to samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation;
and entering the gateway of the Dharma-realm by relying on faith, practice, and vows.
Therefore, when a single thought arises, the myriad spirits take notice;
when faith is born, all Buddhas appear.
As soon as one utters the precious name, the seed is already cast into the womb of the lotus.
Once one has resolved for Bodhi, one is immediately designated by name upon the Golden Land.
Those with the karmic affinity to encounter this will awaken and practice on their own;
those of shallow faith who do not uphold it commit great folly and grave error.
Therefore, it is said that the ultimate proclamation of the One Vehicle culminates in reaching the Land of Bliss,
where the myriad practices are perfected as the most supreme.
By alone invoking the precious name,
the heavy sins of eighty billion kalpas vanish like smoke in an instant,
and the distant reaches of ten trillion lands are traversed as swiftly as a feather’s flight.
When thought and mindfulness are focused, one contemplates the mind and beholds the Buddha-body.
When the mind and its objects interpenetrate, the causal gate gives rise to the supreme fruit.
The pure and impure realms of the ten directions, in their expansion and contraction, are all contained within a single hair-tip.
This single nature is all-encompassing and vast, pervading the entire dharma-realm.
Thus, the Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate one another,
and pure lands and defiled lands communicate in profound harmony.
They mutually cultivate the non-obstruction between phenomena and principle,
like a divine jewel that suddenly contains all treasures,
or like the celestial net where a thousand lights reflect one another.
Since my own mind is thus identical to that of the Buddhas,
one knows that the wandering spirit through billions of lands truly arises within one's own heart;
and how could the conception of form within the nine lotuses escape the span of a single kṣaṇa?
The worthy ones of the Two Vehicles turn their minds and immediately reach the Golden Pond;
ordinary people who have committed the five heinous crimes ascend to the Jewel Realm through ten recitations.
Alas! Consciousness is clouded, hindrances are heavy, faith is meager, and doubt is abundant.
To disparage pure karma as a provisional vehicle and to deride recitation and upholding [the precepts] as coarse practices—
is this not to wallow in the burning house, willingly accepting eternal delusion for kalpas?
How grievous it is that my compassionate parents deeply lament the total waste of this one life!
One must believe that without relying on other power, there is no way to sever karmic afflictions;
and if one does not encounter this gateway, there is no path to liberation from birth and death.
I vow to emulate the former sages and join the company of all Buddhas,
exhorting future worthies to deeply revere this Way.
Having made the vow, I now make it, and I shall continue to make it.
Dedicate every single action to Amitābha;
whether already born, currently being born, or yet to be born,
may every thought-moment return to the Pure Land.
If you wish to accomplish the task of a single lifetime, you should apply your attention right here.
At all times, a thousand chariots shall follow the same ruts;
within the four modes of deportment, ten thousand virtues shall converge.
Together ascend the wondrous gate of Sukhāvatī;
quickly achieve the samādhi of Buddha-recollection.
The first step must be clear and distinct.
"Until one reaches the Western Land, there is no other path.
Regarding Amitābha Buddha’s stage of practice as a bodhisattva, the *Drum-Sound King Sūtra* states:
"In a past kalpa, there was a land named Abhirati."
The king’s name was Kauśika.
His grandfather was King Viśuddhārtha,
and his father was the Cakravartin King Candrotsa.
The mother, of exceptionally beautiful countenance,
gave birth to three sons: the eldest was named Candraprabha,
the next was named Kauśika.
The third is called the Assembly of Emperors.
At that time, there was a Buddha appearing in the world named Lokeśvararāja.
Kauśika conceived the aspiration for the Way,
renounced his royal throne, and went forth under the Buddha,
becoming known as the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Furthermore, the *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states:
"The Bhikṣu Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja,
gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve."
There is no one in all the worlds who can equal him.
At that time, the Buddha spoke of two hundred and ten billion buddha-fields according to his heart’s vow.
Dharmākara bowed his head to the ground and paid homage to the Buddha.
The forty-eight vows are explained in detail; as stated in the original sutra, "If it were not so, I vow not to attain Buddhahood.
At that time, the great earth shook, and wonderful flowers rained down from the sky.
They praised him with one voice, saying, "You will certainly attain Buddhahood.
Regarding the ground of the original vows of Amitābha and Śākyamuni, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states:
In a past kalpa, there was a wheel-turning king named Araṇemin,
who had the great minister Ratnasāgara as his spiritual friend.
At the same time as the Buddha Ratnagarbha, they resolved their minds on Bodhi.
A-raṇemin (Vimalacitta) made this vow:
"I shall practice the Mahāyāna and attain a Pure Land."
I shall never aspire to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in a defiled land where the sentient beings of the world are free from all suffering and affliction;
may I not obtain such a buddha-field.
Thus, he did not attain perfect enlightenment;
now that his fruition is complete and he is titled Amitābha, he manifests in the Pure Land.
Great Minister Ratnasāgara vows to bring sentient beings to maturity within this defiled land.
Now that his fruition is complete, he is titled Śākyamuni;
he has attained the Bodhi of Buddhahood within this defiled and evil world.

For the sake of the noble Queen Vaidehī, the Buddha expounded the primary cause for pure karma. As stated in the *Sūtra on the Meditation on Amitāyus*: "The Buddha, for the sake of the noble Queen Vaidehī, expounded the primary cause for pure karma."
At that time, Vaidehī, weeping aloud, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One,
I pray that you will extensively explain for me the place free from sorrow and affliction."
"I shall be reborn there;
I do not delight in this turbid and evil world of Jambudvīpa.
At that time, the World-Honored One...
He emitted light from between his eyebrows,
which shone throughout immeasurable worlds in the ten directions;
the buddha-fields of all those buddhas appeared within it.
At that time, having seen this,
Vaidehī addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Although these buddha-lands are pure, they all possess radiance."
I now desire to be born in the world of Ultimate Bliss, in the presence of Amitābha Buddha.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will teach me how to contemplate and teach me how to attain right concentration.
The Buddha told Vaidehī:
"Amitābha Buddha is not far from here.
You should fix your mindfulness and contemplate that land with clear attention."
I shall now explain this extensively for you,
so that ordinary persons of the future who cultivate pure karma may be reborn in the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Those who wish to be born in that land:
One should cultivate the three types of merit:
first, filially supporting one's parents and serving one's teachers and elders;
second, practicing compassion by refraining from killing and cultivating the ten wholesome actions.
Second, they receive and uphold the three refuges, fully observe the various precepts, and do not violate the rules of decorum.
Third, they give rise to the bodhicitta, have deep faith in cause and effect, recite Mahāyāna scriptures,
and encourage practitioners to advance on the path.
These three matters are called the true causes for purifying karma.
The Buddha told Ānanda and Vaidehī:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon them well."
Filial piety and support of one's parents, while reciting the Buddha's name, is the essence of all dharmas.
Filial piety is the foremost of all virtuous deeds;
the heart of filiality is itself the Buddha-mind.
Filial conduct is none other than the practice of the Buddha.
If one wishes to attain the Way and become equal to all Buddhas,
one must first practice filial piety and support one's two parents.
Therefore, Master Jizhao said:
"The single character 'filial' (xiao) is the gateway to all wonders.
The Buddha's teaching takes filiality as its fundamental principle."
The Buddhist scriptures take filial piety as their precept;
within these words, there is no obscurity, for they emit the light of the precepts from the mouth.
Directly and clearly, they instantly open the ground of the mind.
Now, filial piety consists of both the filial piety practiced within the household and the filial piety practiced after leaving the household.
As for the filial piety practiced within the household:
When parents love them, they rejoice and do not forget it;
when parents dislike them, they labor for them without resentment.
They follow and comply with their countenances to exhaust themselves in providing for their livelihood.
Regarding filial piety for those who have left the household life:
by severing attachments and bidding farewell to kin, they partake of the subtle to accord with the fundamental;
by penetrating deeply into the principle of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*), they repay the boundless debt of gratitude owed to their parents.
It is the essential path for proceeding toward liberation and the swift shortcut for repaying one's compassionate parents;
it will bring benefit not only in the future.
They also achieved success in their present lives.
Thus, the Son of the Tathāgata crossed the city walls at midnight and completed his path on the Snowy Peaks;
Lu Neng presented gold to his mother.
The Dharma succeeded at Huangmei;
yet, while the Dharma severs worldly ties, one ought to contemplate repaying such virtue.
Thus, [the Buddha] visited his father in Kapilavastu and ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Since it is only right that one personally attend to one's parents even when they have fallen into poverty and lack support,
Piṅgala gave rise to the precept of exhausting one’s heart [in service].
Thus, the Great Master had a hall for his foster mother.
Chen of Muzhou wove sandals to provide for his parents;
Master Lang carried a bundle on his back as he traveled to study.
Thus, those who have left the household life take the flavor of the Dharma as their sweet delicacies.
Without forgetting the heart of returning nourishment to one's parents,
he applied himself diligently to Buddhist affairs while never neglecting the rites of worldly truth.
It is not only the parents of a single lifetime who receive their requital;
rather, the parents of many lifetimes all receive it.
It is not merely the parents of this one body alone.
Thus, all parents throughout the dharma-realm are delivered and ascend together to the shore of enlightenment;
how could this be merely like the Duke of Zhou’s “pairing with Heaven”?
He universally shows the way through the mazes of delusion;
thus, his pure filial piety surpasses that of [Duke] Kao-shu.
How vast indeed is the benefit of the filial piety found in leaving the household life!
If, for instance, the conditions have not yet harmonized or one's parents do not grant permission,
one should exhaustively fulfill the filial piety appropriate for a householder while encouraging the cultivation of the causes for transcending the world.
If one can realize the ultimate truth within the conventional,
there is likewise a path to attaining Buddhahood;
I hope you will return to the conduct of an infant, never failing in the reverence due to your parents.
To repay the labor of their parents’ nurturing care,
they shall reach the stage of the perfection of the One Vehicle,
thereby enabling the lay bodhisattva to practice and understand without doubt.
By this, one may discern the limitations of those eminent transcendents who have left the secular world;
they are unable to fulfill their service to the Buddha,
yet upon witnessing this, they are moved to reflection regarding their service to their parents.
Within this, one can fully realize the practice of filial piety.
Alas! The passage of time is swift, yet parents are difficult to forget.
To have one’s parents dwelling in the hall is like having a Buddha dwelling in the world.
By means of this, one repays the virtue of one's parents and brings to full completion the merit of Buddha-recitation.
Thus we know that when one’s parents rejoice, all Buddhas rejoice.
When this mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure.
It may be said: "The wild scenery is no longer interrupted by mountains;
the moonlight flows directly through to the water."
Regarding serving one's teachers and elders, the ancient worthies said:
"Those who give birth to me are my parents;
those who bring me to completion are my teachers."
A friend is one who knows the teacher; they are the bright guide for those on a mistaken path,
the lamp of wisdom in a dark room,
and the vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering.
The eyes of gods and humans,
whose kindness exceeds that of parents and whose virtue is as weighty as heaven and earth—
this is why a disciple serves their teacher without daring to be negligent or disrespectful.
Have you not seen how they sacrificed their entire bodies to seek half a verse,
severed an arm to strike at the True Vehicle,
and offered their own persons as seats to serve their teachers?
Carrying stones on their waists to grind grain for their ancestors;
selling their hearts and livers to study Prajñāpāramitā;
casting themselves into fires to realize Bodhi.
Compared to the ancients, I am deeply fortunate.
In serving your teacher and studying the Way, how could you not exert yourselves?
You should know that when leaving the mundane world to take refuge in a teacher, one must seek right view.
Those who come from afar to seek instruction must not align themselves with heterodox schools;
they must clarify the causes of sin and merit by carefully discerning the benefits and harms inherent in what is correct and what is false.
Righteousness leads to Buddhahood;
depravity leads to Māra.
If one does not encounter a true master at the outset, one will end up as nothing but a worn-out relic by old age.
For this reason, the Tathāgata knew that the teacher was wrong and departed from him.
The Master chooses what is good and follows it;
observe how the ancient sages were like this.
Why then do people of today not act thus?
All the more so in this final age, where there are many false teachers;
those who wish to practice cultivation must by all means avoid associating with them.
By maintaining right mindfulness, one will ultimately encounter an enlightened teacher;
to fulfill this great destiny, one must be cautious and not take it lightly.
Therefore, a disciple serves their teacher.
This is precisely to act in concert with the Buddha.
It may be called the fourfold offering;
I dare not decline such toil, for even ten thousand taels of gold would be well spent.
I take refuge in the Triple Gem; I take refuge in the Triple Gem. The Buddha is the Great Teacher of the three realms;
the Dharma is the eye of all living beings;
and the Sangha is the superior assembly of the six harmonies.
Together they constitute the truly pure field of merit;
to turn one's back upon them is to be heterodox,
while to accord with them is to be orthodox.
Divine efficacy has no equal;
holy power is inconceivable.
It removes suffering like medicine, as a drum causes arrows to fall and one escapes from peril.
If one breaks through the encirclement with the sword of frost,
suffering is transformed into bliss in an instant,
and the ordinary is transmuted into the sacred in a moment.
Therefore, when the signs of the flaming chariot appear, by taking refuge one immediately attains coolness;
when the earth is about to collapse, by reciting the name all are freed from suffering.
It was through the merit of Puming and the various kings that they were spared from calamity and entered the concentration of emptiness.
It was the power of Prajñā that caused Śakra to retreat before the majesty of Māndhātṛ.
Therefore, sons of faith take refuge in the Triple Gem and offer true compassion,
incense, and flowers to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
By reciting and circulating this Dharma-treasure,
may the merit thus accumulated be dedicated toward Bodhi,
so that all sentient beings may universally attain rebirth together in the Pure Land.
It is not that the *piṅgala* and the parrot attained rebirth in the Western Land merely by chanting;
nor is it that the heavenly kings and emperors, out of reverence, vowed to seek the Holy Path and were all thereby able to ascend to the fruit of Buddhahood.
Below, they are liberated from the wheel of suffering;
it may be said that Chan is the great ocean and poetry is the raw wood.
Of the Great Tang Emperors, there are only three.
To generate the bodhicitta: the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood is called bodhi.
If one generates this mind, one will certainly attain Buddhahood.
The *Vimalacaryā-dharmaparyāya* states:
In practicing the Pure Land, one must skillfully cultivate the aspiration for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
If one practices out of personal aversion to the five turbidities and longing for the nine grades of rebirth, this contradicts the bodhicitta;
such is the conduct of a *śrāvaka* and should not be undertaken.
If, for the sake of sentient beings, one gives rise to great compassion and seeks to go to that land, hoping for swift accomplishment,
then by the power of the Way and supernormal faculties, one will traverse the ten directions.
To rescue and deliver all beings so that they may together attain Buddhahood is to accord with the bodhicitta;
this is the practice of a bodhisattva which one ought to resolve to undertake.
Now, I exhort those of pure karma and noble character who desire to benefit both themselves and others.
One must first resolve the mind and establish one's aspiration before the Triple Gem,
reverently offering incense and flowers,
and with a sincere heart make this vow, saying:
Homage to the Buddha, homage to the Dharma, homage to the Saṅgha.
This disciple, [name], from this day forth,
gives rise to this great resolve, not for the sake of seeking personal blessings or rewards within the realms of humans and devas.
Pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and even bodhisattvas of the provisional vehicles,
relying solely upon the teachings of the Supreme Vehicle, resolve to generate the bodhicitta,
vowing [to do so] for the sake of their parents of this life and their parents of many lifetimes.
May all sentient beings within the dharma-realm, whether enemies or kin, be reborn together in the Pure Land and all attain non-retrogression from *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Recite this three times; at all times and on every day, one must generate this mind and maintain it constantly.
Therefore, Sudhana realized the fruit in a single lifetime;
the dragon girl attained Buddhahood at the age of eight;
and those in the hells who gave rise to the aspiration for enlightenment suddenly transcended the ten stages.
Once a śrāmaṇera has resolved his mind [on enlightenment], he has already transcended the two vehicles;
this may be called a single breath returning to the source, whereby the movement of grace moistens the myriad things deeply.
Having received and upheld the precepts, and having already resolved upon bodhicitta, one should cultivate the practices of a bodhisattva.
First one receives the three refuges;
next one observes the five precepts;
and by gradually cultivating the ten kinds of wholesome dharmas, one brings the threefold aggregate of discipline (tri-saṃvara) to perfection.
When the faculties are mature, one maintains them in their entirety; when the faculties arise, one receives them partially.
There are three auspicious days in each month and six days of fasting (upoṣadha).
If the five precepts are difficult to practice, one may temporarily set aside the two flavors of wine and meat;
if the ten heavy precepts are easy to violate, one may instead observe the single gate of non-killing.
Thus, like fine dust accumulating into a mountain or falling dew adding to a stream, [merit is gradually amassed].
All that descends to the lower slopes ultimately returns to the great ocean.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"While the Buddha was in the world, take the Buddha as your teacher."
After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should take the precepts as one's teacher.
The Brahmajāla Sūtra states:
"The precepts are like the bright sun and moon, and they are also like a necklace of pearls."
By this, multitudes of subtle-dust bodhisattvas attain perfect enlightenment;
thus, dragons are free from the intent to kill,
and wolves possess the resolve to observe the fast.
The monk’s ascetic discipline reached the point of binding grass around his neck;
the householder who protected the geese never drank wine or ate meat throughout his illness.
Thus we know that among all the roots of goodness, the five precepts come first.
The ruler treads upon it to govern the state;
the gentleman upholds it to establish his person.
It must not be set aside even for a moment.
It must not be abandoned for even a moment.
The Buddha calls them the five virtues;
the Confucians call them the five constants.
In the heavens they are the five planets; on earth they are the five sacred peaks;
in humans they are the five viscera;
and in their locations they are the five directions.
To speak more broadly, there is nothing it does not encompass;
whether observing what lies above or examining what lies below, nothing can surpass it.
Thus, the *Fayuan zhulin* states:
What the secular world prizes are benevolence, righteousness, ritual propriety, wisdom, and sincerity;
what the greedy consciousness relies upon are killing, stealing, lust, falsehood, and intoxicants.
Although the paths of the mundane and the sacred diverge, these teachings of gradual instruction are common to both.
Training within the True Dharma must necessarily begin with its causes;
this depends upon the reality of phenomena.
One points directly to the facts, speaking straightforwardly without resorting to ornate rhetoric.
The manifestation of intent through such provisional names is like this:
while practicing the causes without expecting results, the fruits are realized;
from this point one enters the Way, and without longing for pleasure, joy becomes manifest.
Now, one who maintains the precepts and refrains from killing does not seek benevolence, yet benevolence becomes manifest;
one who guards the precepts and refrains from stealing does not rejoice in righteousness, yet righteousness spreads;
one who refrains from sexual misconduct does not pray for propriety, yet propriety is established.
Those who do not engage in falsehood do not seek fame through their faith, yet their faith is exalted;
those who do not drink intoxicants do not practice for the sake of wisdom, yet their wisdom is clarified.
This is not merely a matter of self-restraint and the prevention of wrongdoing, but also serves to assist the state in propagating its transformative teachings.
To cultivate and perfect pure conduct, one must strictly guard the roots of the precepts.
This may be called the harmonious fusion of myriad virtues into a Buddha-land,
a time of great joy and eternal peace.
With a compassionate heart, do not kill; with a compassionate heart, do not kill the insects, fish, birds, beasts, or those born from eggs, wombs, moisture, or transformation.
They are all part of the lineage of future Buddhas, or perhaps were one's own parents over many past lifetimes.
As for those who are filled with dread at the prospect of death and who strive anxiously against a life of poverty—
avoiding suffering and seeking joy for their persons, this sentiment is one and the same;
seeking security and nourishing their lives, this principle is uniform throughout the world.
Why then are they dragged upward with such piteous cries?
Why are they driven toward the ground of death with eyes wide and staring like those upon a butcher’s block?
Some spread nets across the wilds and lay snares throughout the mountains.
The fire followed the ridges according to their elevations;
the smoke grew sparse or dense depending on the terrain.
Hawks as swift as lightning vied to take flight, and horses as fleet as the wind contended to race forward.
The monkey’s soul flees upon seeing the arrow;
the wild goose’s courage falters at the sight of the bow.
The agony of having one's head severed and brain pierced is difficult to endure.
How could the pain that pierces the chest and penetrates the bones be restrained?
Moreover, these beings all receive the five elements and together contain the four phenomena;
they equally partake of the Buddha-nature and share in spiritual intelligence.
Why then do you present these mountains of flesh and set up these braziers of fire?
You fill your own bellies and gratify your hearts with such delicacies,
yet you remain utterly unaware that those who sever life are [committing this atrocity].
This is the shedding of the Buddha’s own blood.
Those who eat his flesh are surely consuming the bodies of their own parents;
they commit the profound transgression of killing and sever the seed-nature of compassion.
Before birth, one's merit and longevity are consumed in secret;
after death, one sinks into the depths of the mountains of knives and trees of swords,
becoming once again a chicken, a pig, a fish, or a rabbit.
The sequence of repayment extends even to the act of slaughtering, cooking, and roasting; cause and effect are thus analogous.
To contemplate the eating of meat with clarity is truly enough to make one’s heart tremble with cold.
Even if it is sold and traded at the butcher’s gate, one cannot escape the grave retribution.
A bodhisattva would rather break his own bones than ever eat the flesh of a living being.
Thus, when the white hare burned his body, the immortal did not look upon it with indifference;
since he would not even pluck a blade of grass, how could he possibly tolerate [the eating of] flesh?
When one returns to the kitchen, there is the instruction of "hearing the sound and not being able to bear it," which teaches compassionate cultivation.
To sell what others have killed while eating it with a mind of complicity is a grave offense;
thus, the Great Sage bestowed his compassion by establishing precepts to forever sever the taking of life, for the merit of this is immense.
Those who cultivate the Pure Land and thus maintain their ancient halls may be said to be like dragons in a verdant pool who do not crave the taste of fragrant bait.
Only then are they true dragons of the deep abyss.
Cultivating the Ten Wholesome Karmas: As for the profound essentials of the Mahāyāna, they fundamentally do not depart from the single mind.
Since the primary cause for purifying karma must first involve the cultivation of the ten wholesome deeds.
Having severed the sevenfold transgressions of body and speech,
these seven practices are perfected;
having extinguished the roots of the three poisons within the mental consciousness.
The three trainings are fully contained herein;
they are what those seeking the Pure Land within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* ought to cultivate,
and they are what those on the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*) within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are able to personally realize.
From humans and devas up to the Peak of Existence, the ten wholesome actions serve as the condition for rebirth.
From the śrāvaka vehicle up to the Buddha vehicle, the ten wholesome actions constitute the foundation for entering the Path.
Failing to follow the Buddha’s precepts is the primary gateway to falling into the three miserable realms;
even if one obtains a human body, one will incur two kinds of evil retributions, namely,
the failure to cultivate the ten wholesome paths and the practice of the ten unwholesome paths.
To uphold these as the dharma-gate of the ten precepts is truly the foundation for the Pure Land;
I universally exhort you to constantly practice this conduct,
for it is the Dharma-garden of the Bodhisattvas.
It is fitting that they be established therein so that they may reach the great city of fearlessness and ascend to the stage of non-retrogression;
how could their merit ever be measured?
O Son of the Buddha, this is why you must study:
with deep faith in cause and effect, and with deep faith in cause and effect, you should set foot upon the profound path and cleanse your mind in the Great Way;
have deep faith in the causes and effects of the mundane world.
One must thoroughly investigate the source of transcendence from the world;
in seeking to exhaust that source, one must preserve its essential core.
As for that which is essential and functional, does it not lie within the Dharma of the mind?
The mind encompasses all myriad practices and unifies all manifold phenomena.
Because the mind has no fixed nature, it alternately employs both good and evil, taking sin and merit as its shadows and echoes; thus, cause and effect do not contradict one another.
Thus we know that movement in response to objects is called the cause (*hetu*);
the arising of consciousness from such movement is called the condition (*pratyaya*).
When conditions arise, there is the characteristic of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*).
According to the karma one possesses, the retribution is certain. Therefore,
wholesome and unwholesome actions are the causes of the world,
while the three realms, the six paths, the nine abodes, and the four modes of birth are the fruits of the world.
The practice of the Buddha-remembrance method (nien-fo) is the cause for transcending the world;
being born through transformation in the nine grades within the Pure Land and attaining Buddhahood is the fruit of transcending the world.
Because they clearly understand the aforementioned causes and effects within their minds,
they do not take pleasure in or become attached to worldly phenomena;
regarding supramundane phenomena, their mental activity does not conflict with them.
One's every thought is ever-present in the Pure Land;

That which sentient beings inherently possess cannot be obtained through artificial effort.
That the secret treasury remains unmanifest is because it is shrouded by the three delusions.
Ignorance obscures the dharma-nature.
The dust-like afflictions (kleśa) obstruct transformation and guidance;
the views and thoughts (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāva-kleśa) hinder emptiness and stillness.

destroys the three delusions,

The contemplation of the conventional (parikalpita-svabhāva) destroys the delusions as numerous as motes of dust;
it realizes the knowledge of the modes of phenomena (dharmākārajñatā) and accomplishes the virtue of liberation.
The contemplation of the middle (madhyama-pratītyasamutpāda) destroys the delusion of ignorance (avidyā).
The realization of all-aspect wisdom and the accomplishment of the merit of the Dharma-body are not separate,
nor do they occur at different times.
Because the principle of nature is inherent in all phenomena;
yet these three truths are such by their very nature.

Therefore, while it differs from the Chan school, it is not different from it.
When a practitioner recollects the Buddha, the mental faculty serves as the cause,
and the white tuft of hair and the circular halo serve as the conditions.

and the mind will arise as the visualization of the Buddha.
This is merely a provisional designation.
Its essence is empty yet luminously penetrating.

It is the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha through the perception of emptiness, the dharma-gate of non-conceptualization, the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha through the perception of emptiness, the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha through the perception of emptiness, and the dharma-gate of non-conceptualization. As for the samādhi of contemplating the Buddha through the perception of emptiness:
As the Patriarch’s Preface states:
"When thought is focused and visualization is tranquil, the will becomes singular and undisturbed;
when the vital energy is empty and the spirit is luminous, there is nothing obscure that is not penetrated."
One who enters this samādhi becomes oblivious and forgets all cognition;
worldly burdens are instantly eliminated and obstructed emotions melt into clarity.

To enter this contemplation is to discern the true reality.

First, contemplate that all phenomena are provisional,
even down to the four great elements, the five aggregates, the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses;

Internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, and the emptiness of emptiness itself are likewise unattainable.
In this way, one suddenly enters the Tathāgata’s jewel-bright ocean of emptiness,
wherein the nature of awareness is true emptiness.
This is because the emptiness of the Tathāgatagarbha is perfectly luminous and its numinous light universally illumines the nature of the Dharma-realm;
it is like a mani jewel that produces whatever is desired,
and like the great ocean, deep and vast, which contains and encompasses all.
The Wisdom of Equality is called the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

The Dharma Gate of Single-Minded Contemplation of the Buddha through the Samādhi of Daily Recollection of the Buddha. The *Sūtra on the Visualization of the Buddha of Immeasurable Life* states:
The Buddha addressed Vaidehī:
You and all sentient beings should concentrate your minds;
fix your mindfulness on a single point and direct your thoughts toward the western direction.
As for those who practice such visualization:
All sentient beings, unless they are born blind,
possess eyes and all see the sun set; therefore,
one should give rise to this thought and sit facing directly west.
Observe the sun with careful attention, causing the mind to remain firm and the visualization to be unwavering.
When the sun is about to set, its form will appear like a suspended drum.
Once you have seen the sun, whether with eyes open or closed, ensure it remains clearly manifest.
This is the visualization of the sun;
it is called the first contemplation.
A practitioner who enters this contemplation must stay in a quiet place, cutting off all external conditions.
Sitting upright and collecting the mind, one contemplates the solar disc as it appears directly before one's eyes.
Focusing the mind on a single object, one remains motionless and tranquil,
like beholding the reflection of one's own face in a clear mirror.
If the mind wanders and scatters, restrain it and cause it to return;
when the mind rests and abides in concentration,
one immediately attains samādhi.
One may call this the golden crow at the bottom of the sea and the sun in the heavens;
the pupil in the eye and the person before one.
Regarding the ultimate dharma-gate of the samādhi of Chan and Buddha-recitation, the *Preface to the Chan Sūtra* by the Distant Patriarch states:
Without wisdom, meditation cannot exhaustively fathom its stillness;
without meditation, wisdom cannot deepen its illumination.
Meditation and wisdom are defined as illumination and stillness, and they are mutually complementary.
Illumination is not separate from stillness;
stillness is not separate from illumination.
When there is resonance, they move together.
When responding, they share the same destination.
Compassionate illumination is described as "ever-illuminating while remaining quiescent" and "ever-quiescent while illuminating."
Perpetually tranquil and perpetually illuminating—
this is called the Buddha of Constant Tranquil Light;
those who wish to practice Chan to see their nature should rely solely on this method.
One must sit upright with the body straight in a quiet room;
sweep away external conditions and burdens, sever the dust of the passions,
and keep the eyes wide open so as not to be attached to external objects.
Without dwelling in internal concentration,
one turns the light back for a single illumination;
then both within and without are simultaneously stilled.
Thereafter, maintain a state of quiet intimacy;
whenever a thought arises, silently recite "Namo Amitābha Buddha" three or five times.
Turn the light back upon yourself and look within, saying, "This is the seeing of one's nature."
Then, who is it that ultimately attains Buddhahood?
It is this very nature of mine, Amitābha.
Furthermore, look closely at what you are currently raising [in mind].
From where does this single thought arise? Examine and break through this single thought.

Furthermore, observe thus and investigate thus, applying yourself with urgency to the practice without allowing for interruption;
remain alert and clear-minded, never becoming obscured.
It is like a hen brooding her eggs; it does not matter whether one is engaged in any of the four postures.
Thus lift up [the mind], thus look, and thus investigate.
Suddenly, while walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, when hearing sounds or seeing forms—

he personally beheld the Buddha Amitābha as his own original nature;

In stillness, there is no lack of illumination; in movement, one does not depart from quiescence.

without an intervening thought or a divergent thought,

This may be called "When One Thing Is Understood, Ten Thousand Matters Are Complete.

"The Transformation Buddha comes to welcome you, the Transformation Buddha comes to welcome you. From the *Zongjing Lu* (Record of the Source Mirror), it is asked:

The Dharmakāya, the true Buddha, is fundamentally without birth or extinction;
from this reality it gives rise to transformations to guide those with deluded faculties.
Since transformation is itself reality, the real and the responsive are of one and the same limit.
That is to say, it neither comes nor goes, responding in accordance with the minds of sentient beings.
Furthermore, since the manifested body is itself the Truth (tathatā), it is said to have no coming or going;
yet, as a manifestation flowing forth from the Truth, it appears to have movement and return.

it is seen without the characteristic of being seen.
Coming without coming is like the moon suddenly appearing.

Exhortation to Practice in Advance for the Ten Matters of the Time of Death, Should One Fail to Achieve Mindfulness at the Final Moment: Ordinary beings, burdened by heavy karma, crave life in every circumstance.

Someone asked:

"Why should one not cultivate superior karma in advance?
He replied,

Some may fall into a state of illness and delirium,
while others may suddenly pass away prematurely; in either case,
they will lack the wholesome roots cultivated during their lifetime.
It is difficult to escape the calamities of future lives;
one must therefore prepare virtuous conditions in advance,
for fear of such transgressions.
There are ten circumstances at the time of death when one is unable to practice mindfulness of the Buddha:
first, one may not necessarily encounter virtuous friends;
second, one may be beset by illness and suffering such that the spirit is clouded and the nature is disordered.
Third, those who have lost the power of speech due to a stroke and are unable to utter their names;
fourth, those who are deranged and have lost their minds, making it difficult to focus their thoughts with concentration;
fifth, those who encounter water or fire and have no leisure to maintain sincere devotion.
Sixth, suddenly encountering tigers or wolves, one becomes terrified and flustered.
Seventh, at the critical moment, evil companions destroy one's resolve for the Path.
Eighth, eating to excess until satiated leads to confusion and loss of life.
Ninth, those who suddenly perish in the midst of military conflict or battle;
tenth, those who fall from high cliffs and lose their lives through injury.
Thus, one should know that at the moment of death, it is difficult to guarantee whether the outcome will be auspicious or inauspicious.
One must practice in advance;
this can be called "preparing during leisure for use in times of urgency," so as to avoid being flustered and手忙腳亂 (in a state of frantic confusion) when the critical moment arrives.
